chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Bazīʿ, from Muḥammad ibn al-Fuḍayl, from Abū al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Kinānī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:

There were boys in the time of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib عليه السلام playing with their throwing-sticks. One of them threw his stick and broke the lateral incisor of his companion. The matter was brought before Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام, and the thrower established proof that he had said, ‘Beware!’ So Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام waived qiṣāṣ, then said: ‘He who warned has excused himself.’
He said: And I asked him about a man whom qiṣāṣ kills—does he have diyah? He said: ‘If that were so, no one would ever exact qiṣāṣ from anyone; and whoever is killed by the hadd has no diyah.’

key_terms.أَعْذَرَ: became excused by giving sufficient prior warning
key_terms.الْبَيِّنَةَ: legal proof or evidentiary testimony establishing a claim
key_terms.الْحَدُّ: a prescribed legal punishment in the Sacred Law
key_terms.الْقِصَاصَ: retaliatory legal punishment for equivalent bodily injury or killing
key_terms.دِيَةٌ: financial compensation owed for unlawful killing or injury

ai.seo_question: Is diyah owed when someone is lawfully killed by qiṣāṣ or hadd, and does a prior warning remove liability for injury?
ai.summary: This hadith records a judicial ruling connected to accidental injury during play in the time of Amīr al-Muʾminīn ʿAlī عليه السلام. It establishes that when adequate warning was given, qiṣāṣ was not enforced, and it also states that one lawfully killed by qiṣāṣ or hadd is not entitled to diyah.
